source.title: Asymptotics of Learning with Deep Structured (Random) Features
source.authors: Dominik Schröder; Daniil Dmitriev; Hugo Cui; Bruno Loureiro

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no evident truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates test-error learning curves for readout regression across training times and sample complexities, using its own theoretical and empirical methods rather than reproducing the original double-descent experiments.
record.gate_note: The introduction mentions double descent as a phenomenon captured in prior work, but that is cited background, not a result of this study. The study's own figures vary training time and sample complexity; the text gives one qualitative training-time observation, but does not state whether test error peaks near an interpolation threshold or rises as sample size increases.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only as cited background ([1]) in the introduction. The study's own results are about whether its asymptotic ridge-readout formula matches simulated learning curves. The text never states a double-descent peak, a more-data-hurts region or an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall in its own results. The one training-time observation is readout-regression error on saved feature snapshots at optimal λ, a different construct from a model's test error over epochs. Fig. 5 mentions an interpolation threshold shifting, but the curve shape is figure-only and unreadable.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors give a tight asymptotic test-error formula for ridge regression on Lipschitz feature maps, and a closed-form linearized covariance for Gaussian rainbow networks (proved for two layers). They find heuristically that the formula also captures readout learning curves of some lazily trained networks, on synthetic and MNIST data. They draw no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes ridge regression on fixed or trained feature maps and compares theoretical predictions with numerical learning curves; it does not reproduce the original double-descent sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported learning curves vary with training time, sample complexity, and regularization; the text notes that the interpolation threshold shifts during training.

fits_no_version.finding: Ridge-readout error on MNIST-trained feature snapshots, at optimal λ, first worsens early in training, then improves well beyond initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Readout-regression performance on learned features is non-monotonic over backbone training time.

record.problems: For the claim-relevant curves, the supplied text gives no numerical values, uncertainty estimates, or textual description of whether the sample-complexity curves rise near interpolation. The training-time observation does not establish a complete double-descent shape.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the many sample-complexity curves in Figs. 2–7: the text does not provide their individual plotted values or enough condition-specific outcomes to extract separate results.

untested.parts: No network test error tracked over epochs for a peak.
Sample-wise curves exist only in figures; no stated rise with more data.
No result on a second descent past interpolation across model classes.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
Noise and regularization are varied in figures, but no stated result on peak dependence or its removal.

missing.what: Fixed-λ learning curves versus sample size n across training snapshots, with a stated leftward shift of the interpolation threshold. Plotted values are needed to judge any sample-wise peak or more-data-hurts region.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory paper. Its interpolation-threshold behaviour is visible only in figures; the text never states it as a result. Consider re-examining Fig. 5 if the figure values become available.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size is reported.
The text does not report a complete fall-rise-fall curve over epochs or locate a peak at interpolation.
Sample complexity is varied, but the supplied text does not expose the plotted values or state whether more data raises test error near interpolation.
No comparison of double-descent curves across model classes is reported.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed as predicting peak locations across axes.
The study does not test whether noise or regularization drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The study does not assess whether an effective parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.measure: test error of readout feature regression across training time
rows.value: The text states that feature-regression performance first deteriorates and later improves beyond initialization; no numerical values are stated.
rows.note: This reports a nonmonotonic training-time change, but not the full fall-rise-fall pattern or an error peak near interpolation.
rows.check: The condition is wrong: Fig. 6 belongs to the MNIST experiments (App. C.2), not the synthetic Gaussian data. The measure is ridge-readout error on feature snapshots at optimal λ, not the trained network's test error over epochs, so it is not V2's construct. The pattern described is deterioration then improvement relative to initialization, not fall-rise-fall. Under optimal regularization it also cannot show a V2 peak.
